stops.name: Concepción, the proclamation of independence
stops.campa: On the first day of 1818, in the plaza of Concepción with Osorio's invasion fleet already at sea, O'Higgins proclaims what the cautious have postponed for eight years: Chile is, and of right ought to be, free. The Act is dated this day from Concepción: the declaration made not from a safe capital but from the war's front porch, an answer flung at the approaching enemy. The canon relishes the defiance of the timing: independence declared precisely when Spain comes strongest to prevent it.
stops.quote: La fuerza ha sido la razón suprema que por más de trescientos años ha mantenido al Nuevo Mundo en la necesidad de venerar como un dogma la usurpación de sus derechos.
stops.quote_source: Acta de la Independencia de Chile, dated Concepción, 1 January 1818, issued and signed by O'Higgins as Supreme Director

stops.name: Talca, the oath sworn in the house of his childhood
stops.campa: On 12 February 1818, first anniversary of Chacabuco, O'Higgins signs and swears the Declaration of Independence at Talca, in the very house of Juan Albano where he lived as a nameless child; the same day, before the delegate director in Santiago's plaza, the whole people raise their right hands. The circle the canon drew at his cradle closes: the room that sheltered the huacho witnesses the birth certificate of the nation. Bells, salvos and Te Deums run the length of the valley while Osorio's army marches north against the newborn state.
stops.quote: Juro a Dios y prometo a la patria, bajo la garantía de mi honor, vida y fortuna, sostener la presente declaración de independencia.
stops.quote_source: Oath formula of the Jura de la Independencia, 12 February 1818

stops.name: Cancha Rayada, the night of the shattered arm
stops.campa: On the night of 19 March 1818, at Cancha Rayada outside Talca, Osorio's veterans fall on the patriot camp in the dark. The army is thrown into chaos; guns are lost; a musket ball shatters O'Higgins's right arm as he tries to stem the rout. Word runs to Santiago that the army is destroyed, that San Martín is dead, that O'Higgins is dead. But Las Heras brings three thousand men off unbroken, and the wounded Director, refusing amputation, rides north with his arm in a sling to show himself alive. The nation holds its breath.

stops.name: Santiago, 'Aún tenemos patria, ciudadanos'
stops.campa: Panic empties Santiago's strongboxes toward Mendoza until Manuel Rodríguez, the guerrillero of the lodge, wheels his horse in the plaza and cries that there is still a fatherland, citizens, and raises a regiment of clerks and artisans, the Húsares de la Muerte, in an afternoon. Into this fevered city rides O'Higgins, gray with pain, his arm bound, and the sight of the living Director turns terror into fury. He pours every man and peso toward the plain of Maipo where San Martín reassembles the army for the final throw.

stops.name: The plain of Maipú, the battle and the abrazo
stops.campa: On 5 April 1818 San Martín breaks Osorio's army on the plain of Maipú in the decisive battle of the south. O'Higgins, forbidden by his wound to command, cannot stay away: at the crisis of the afternoon he arrives from Santiago at the head of a thousand militia, his arm in a sling, and rides through the smoke to San Martín. He throws his good arm around the victor's neck with the words the two nations have repeated ever since; San Martín answers that Chile will never forget the illustrious invalid who came to the field in such a state. The embrace of Maipú seals the freedom of Chile.
stops.quote_source: The Abrazo de Maipú, 5 April 1818, as recorded in the battle tradition (Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano; Barros Arana)

stops.name: Valparaíso, the First National Squadron sails
stops.campa: O'Higgins has begged, taxed and mortgaged a navy into existence: four ships bought and armed at a bankrupt nation's cost. On 10 October 1818 the First National Squadron under Blanco Encalada stands out of Valparaíso to hunt the Spanish convoy, and the Director watches from the height above the port. Turning to those beside him he speaks the sentence the Armada keeps as its founding prophecy, measuring Columbus's three caravels against his own four hulls. Within the month the squadron takes the frigate María Isabel and the sea begins to change owners.
stops.quote: Tres barquichuelos dieron a los reyes de España la posesión del Nuevo Mundo; estas cuatro tablas van a quitársela.
stops.quote_source: Tradition of the Armada de Chile, departure of the First National Squadron, 10 October 1818

stops.name: Valparaíso, Cochrane comes to the flag
stops.campa: On 28 November 1818 Lord Thomas Cochrane, the sea-wolf of the Aix Roads, steps ashore at Valparaíso to take command of the squadron O'Higgins has built for him. The Director gives the Radical Lord his fleet and his mission: sweep the Pacific, break Callao, prepare the water road to Lima. Between the huaso Director and the Scottish firebrand there will be storms of pride and pay. The canon does not hide them. But under their joined hands Chile becomes, for one blazing decade, the naval power of the Pacific.

stops.name: Valparaíso, the Liberating Expedition of Peru sails
stops.campa: On 20 August 1820, his forty-second birthday, O'Higgins stands above Valparaíso as the Liberating Expedition of Peru puts to sea: Cochrane's warships shepherding sixteen transports, San Martín and four thousand soldiers bound for the coast of the Viceroyalty. It is the largest armament the new world's south has ever launched, paid for by Chile's last peso, the fulfilment of the design drawn in Mendoza and, further back, in Miranda's rooms at Grafton Way. The Director watches the sails diminish toward the destiny of a continent, and the canon fixes him there: the giver of the fleet, remaining behind.

stops.name: Santiago, the builder's years and the gathering shadows
stops.campa: The Director builds as he fought, frontally: the Alameda de las Delicias laid out over the old river branch, the Escuela Militar, the Cementerio General consecrated in 1821, the markets, the night watch, the abolition of titles of nobility and of bullfights, ships and schools. But the ledger of the lodge has dark entries the canon does not conceal: Manuel Rodríguez shot at Til Til, the Carrera brothers dead before Mendoza firing squads, and the aristocracy he has humbled whispering in every parlor. The hero of Rancagua governs a peace more treacherous than any siege.

stops.name: Santiago, the Constitution of 1822 and the storm
stops.campa: In October 1822 a convention promulgates a new Constitution that could prolong the Director's rule for years, and the country's patience breaks. Concepción rises behind General Freire; the provinces disown the capital; the treasury is empty from paying for Peru's liberation, and an earthquake has flattened Valparaíso as if the ground itself voted. O'Higgins, the man who charged at Chacabuco without orders, now faces the one enemy that cannot be charged: the turning of his own people. The canon sets the scene for the noblest act of his life.

stops.name: Santiago, sala del Consulado, the abdication and the bared chest
stops.campa: On 28 January 1823, before an open cabildo of two hundred notables in the hall of the Consulado, O'Higgins lays down the supreme power rather than light a civil war. He swears in the junta that replaces him, then turns to the assembly that has muttered accusations for months, tears open his uniform coat, and offers them his bare chest: if his faults must be purged in blood, let them take their vengeance now. The hall that came to depose him erupts instead in vivas. He walks out a private citizen, greater in the fall, says the canon, than in all his victories.
stops.quote: Estoy dispuesto a contestar todas las acusaciones que se me hagan; y si esas faltas han causado desgracias que no pueden purgarse más que con mi sangre, tomad de mí la venganza que queráis. Aquí está mi pecho.
stops.quote_source: Abdication speech, cabildo abierto of Santiago, 28 January 1823 (Barros Arana; Academia de Historia Militar de Chile)

stops.name: Valparaíso, embarking on the brig Fly
stops.campa: Held half a year under courteous guard while his enemies audit his rule and find nothing to seize, O'Higgins is at last permitted to go. On 17 July 1823 he boards the English brig Fly at Valparaíso with his mother, his sister Rosa and his small son Demetrio, bound for Peru, he says for a season, for his health. The hills of the port drop below the horizon. He is forty-four years old, and he will never see Chile again. The canon marks the third sea-crossing, the one with no return.
